message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
## Review: Weekend Rate Restructure

**Bottom line.** A rate increase is probably justified: you're priced below every competitor, and the arithmetic shows occupancy has a fair cushion before revenue suffers. But the paper's two main supports don't hold up as presented:
- **The "direct test" of price sensitivity is confounded.** The June-to-July rise is the hotel's normal seasonal pattern.
- **The £204,000 is not a floor.** It uses 124 rooms when the hotel has 112, and it assumes every weekend room is sold at the full public rate.

The two-night minimum also conflicts with the hotel's largest Saturday business, wedding guests who stay one night. That makes it a downside risk, not unquantified upside.

### 1. The price-sensitivity "test" is seasonal

The BAR rose at the end of June 2025, and weekend occupancy went from 81% in June to 89% in July. But the paper itself explains why July is strong: the harbour festival and school holidays. August reached 93% with no further price change. A rise from June to July is what the hotel would expect in any year.

To test the effect of price, compare **July–September 2025 with the same months in 2024**, when the rate was £135. If occupancy held or rose year on year, that's real evidence. The month-to-month comparison isn't.

The value-for-money score of 8.4 is also partly a *result* of being the cheapest hotel in the set. At £165 you'd match the cheapest competitor, so expect that score to fall rather than treat it as headroom.

### 2. The revenue estimate is overstated

**Room count.** Section 2 says 112 rooms, while Section 5 uses 124.

| | Calculation | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| As stated (124 rooms) | 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 | £203,800 |
| Correct room count (112) | 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 | **£184,000** |

**Not all rooms are sold at BAR.** Several kinds of booking won't get the extra £20, or not all of it:
- contracted corporate and group rates, which are honoured;
- wedding blocks, around 38% of Saturdays, likely on group rates;
- packages and discounts;
- online travel agent (OTA) commission, typically 15–20% of the rate.

The real gain could be well below £184,000. Show the share of weekend room nights actually sold at BAR, and the net rate after commission.

**VAT.** Check whether the figure includes the 20% VAT on room rates. Revenue is usually reported net of VAT.

**First-year timing.** Many June stays will already be booked at £145, so the gain in the first year will be smaller.

### 3. The two-night minimum conflicts with wedding business

The paper's own data:
- **38% of Saturday-night bookings** are wedding guests who arrive Saturday and check out Sunday.
- The minimum applies to *any* stay including a Saturday.

As written, these guests either can't book or must pay for a second night they don't want. Either way, many will go elsewhere, and the couples organising the room blocks may move them to competitors next year. Groups "already contracted" are protected, but future wedding blocks aren't mentioned.

A blanket minimum can also lose bookings on the **21 Saturdays that didn't sell out**. On those nights, a guest who wants only Saturday is turned away from a room that would otherwise stay empty.

Both risks have a common fix: **apply the minimum only on dates forecast to sell out**, and **exempt wedding and group blocks**. Until the minimum is quantified with those safeguards, it's a risk, not hidden upside. Calling £204,000 "a floor rather than a target", as the author does, doesn't hold.

### 4. A point in the proposal's favour that it doesn't make

Revenue per available room on weekends is £145 × 79% = £114.55. At £165, the hotel keeps that revenue as long as occupancy stays above 114.55 ÷ 165 ≈ **69%**. Occupancy can fall about **10 points**, or about 12% of its current level, before the change loses revenue. That's a reasonable margin of safety, and the paper should show it.

On this basis, the monitoring trigger of a five-point fall is suitably cautious. The trigger is monthly and backward-looking, though, so the weekly pick-up review should be the early warning. If forward bookings are running behind, act on the trend before the month's figures arrive.

### What holds up

- Pricing below the whole competitive set is well evidenced, and a rate increase is reasonable.
- Average 2025 occupancy (79.2%) and the room-night count (104) are correct.
- Corporate and contracted group rates are protected.
- Weekly monitoring of pick-up against 2025 is a good basis for tracking the change.

### Recommended changes

1. Replace the June-to-July comparison with a year-on-year one, July–September 2025 against 2024.
2. Recalculate the revenue on 112 rooms, using the share of nights sold at BAR, net of commission and VAT. Present it as an estimate with a range, not a floor.
3. Add the break-even occupancy (about 69%) to show the margin of safety.
4. Restrict the two-night minimum to high-demand dates, and exempt wedding and group blocks. Otherwise, model the likely loss of wedding business.
5. Act on weekly pick-up data rather than waiting for the monthly trigger.

The rate increase looks sound. The two-night minimum, as drafted, could lose the hotel more than it gains.
